vulnerabilities: Macroeconomic and currency instability — persistent high inflation, currency depreciation, and foreign debt exposure reduce fiscal room to sustain major defence acquisition programmes long-term

Energy import dependence — heavy reliance on imported natural gas and crude oil from Russia, Azerbaijan, and Iran drives a large trade deficit and exposes Türkiye to supply cutoffs during regional disputes

Friction with NATO partners over defence procurement — historical reliance on Western aviation/missile systems collided with the F-35 programme exclusion (following Türkiye's S-400 purchase from Russia) and US CAATSA sanctions
Complex southern security border (Syria, Iraq) — direct exposure to cross-border non-state armed groups, refugee flows, and instability drains land forces and domestic security resources
Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean maritime disputes — overlapping territorial-water and EEZ claims with Greece and Cyprus carry a real risk of naval standoff and restrict energy exploration access
strengths: Sole legal and physical authority over the Turkish Straits (Bosphorus/Dardanelles) under the 1936 Montreux Convention — controls all Black Sea naval ingress/egress
Autonomous domestic UAV and defence industry — mass-produced, combat-proven drones (Bayraktar TB2/TB3, Akinci) sold across the Middle East, Europe, and Africa
Cross-regional geographic/logistics pivot — central corridor for energy pipelines and rail links connecting Central Asia/Caucasus to Europe
NATO's second-largest standing military force, capable of multi-theatre operations (Syria, Iraq, Libya, Caucasus)
Multi-vector diplomatic mediation capacity — able to conduct high-level diplomacy simultaneously with Moscow, Kyiv, Western capitals, and Middle Eastern governments
